title: Fit the last piece into a jigsaw puzzle
instruction: Put the last piece into the jigsaw puzzle.
context: Jigsaw puzzles are among the most common pastimes, and most people have put the last piece into one. Nothing has to be chosen or recognised here: there is one piece and one gap, and the difficulty is all in the hand. The piece is a flat wooden piece 6.35 mm thick lying on the table, so it can only be pinched by its edges with the fingertips down at the table, clear of its knobs. It has to be turned the one way it fits and brought down squarely: the edges are square-cut, with no chamfer and half a millimetre of play, so a piece set down a little turned or off-centre rides up on a knob instead of dropping in. Then it is pressed flat.
setup: Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them; heights are above the table. Two arms (bases 61 cm apart), one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. (1) A wooden jigsaw puzzle laser-cut from 1/4 in (6.35 mm) birch plywood, 30 x 30 cm in 10 x 10 classic knob-and-hole pieces about 3 cm across, finished except for one piece, lying picture up on the bare table with its rows square to the table's front edge. The gap is the second piece in from the puzzle's right-hand edge, in the fifth row from the robot, and is centred 34 cm forward on the centre line; so the puzzle's right-hand edge is 4.5 cm to the right of the gap's middle. Only the puzzle within 7.5 cm of the gap is modelled; the rest is drawn. (2) The last piece, loose, 6.35 mm thick, about 4 g: a body 3.0 cm square, with a knob on three sides and a hole on the fourth. Each knob has a neck 6 mm wide and a round head 8.4 mm across, centred 6.8 mm out from the edge; the hole is the same shape, cut in. In the finished puzzle its hole faces the robot, round the knob of the piece in front of it (nearer the robot), and its knobs point left, away from the robot and right. It lies picture up on the table with its middle 9.5 cm to the right of the gap's middle and 33.5 cm forward, turned a quarter turn clockwise (seen from above) from the way it fits, so its hole faces left. Between the piece and its gap there is 0.5 mm of play all round. The piece's nearest edge is 3.5 cm from the puzzle's right-hand edge. Nothing else is on the table. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Measured at the end of the run, with the piece still. 1.0: the piece is seated in its gap: its middle within 1.5 mm of the gap's middle, turned within 4 degrees of the way it fits, flat within 3 degrees and down within 0.8 mm of the table, so level with the pieces round it; and each hand's grip point (midway between its fingertips) is at least 3 cm from the piece's middle. 0.75: seated, but a hand still on it. 0.5: in its gap the right way round (within 4 mm and 10 degrees) but not down flat, e.g. a knob riding on a neighbour. 0.25: over its gap the right way round (within 6 mm and 10 degrees) but resting on the puzzle. 0.0: anything else, e.g. still where it started, put down turned the wrong way, or dropped. In a real trial: a photo from straight above to check the piece's place and turn, and a straightedge laid across the piece and its neighbours; a seated piece leaves no gap under the straightedge.
reset_notes: Lift the piece out of its gap and lay it back picture up on its mark, 9.5 cm to the right of the gap, turned a quarter turn clockwise (hole facing left). Check that the pieces round the gap have not moved; nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1 with PhysX, 20 Hz control). The piece and the puzzle round its gap are rigid; in plan view their outlines are built from 0.5 mm strips, so the knobs' round heads are stepped by about 0.1 mm. The wood's grain, the laser-cut edges' slight taper and the picture are not modelled. The finished puzzle is fixed in place (a real one can shift a little if pushed). Cameras render at 320 x 176.
